rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about any design axis (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion). The most critical unknown is whether the basic RNA signal alone provides any useful classification performance, and what magnitude of accuracy to expect. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable baseline. It isolates the question 'does a linear 2000-dim PCA reduction of single-profile RNA data yield meaningful signal?' without confounding from learned encoders, image data, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Establishing this minimal baseline is the standard and most information-efficient first step in sequential design. It is computationally cheap (PCA is fast, no image pipeline), provides a reference point against which every subsequent experiment (learned encoders, multiprofile, image, multimodal) can be compared, and helps calibrate the performance landscape before investing budget in more complex configurations. Without this anchor, later comparisons would lack a clear attribution of where gains (or losses) originate.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal for this task at all. This is the most consequential design decision: it determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and which branch of the configuration space to prioritize. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001—same profile setting, same structural simplicity (no aggregation/fusion needed)—isolating the effect of modality. If image-only substantially outperforms RNA-only, multimodal fusion configs become high-priority; if it underperforms, we should invest in RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) instead. ResNet50 is a standard, well-calibrated image encoder appropriate for a first modality probe. Under a tight budget, resolving which modality is stronger before committing to complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations is the highest-information-value next step.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8% acc, making RNA the clearly dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA encoder tested (linear PCA). Question: Does a learned, biologically-informed RNA representation (scvi_n200) outperform linear PCA in capturing task-relevant structure? This is a clean single-variable change from config_001 (same model_setting, same profile_setting, only encoder differs), isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why best next experiment: Since RNA is the stronger modality, improving its representation has the highest expected payoff. If scvi_n200 improves over PCA, it validates learned representations and makes the many multimodal scvi configurations (config_028-039) high-value follow-ups. If it does not improve, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward multiprofile/aggregation or fusion design. This single experiment reduces the largest current uncertainty about the most impactful design axis.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520) clearly outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) for single-profile RNA, and image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), suggesting RNA is the dominant signal. The multiprofile design axis is completely untested. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (with simple avgpool) improve upon the best single-profile RNA result (config_004, scvi_n200, 0.520)? This isolates the multiprofile effect using the strongest encoder identified so far and the simplest aggregation, avoiding confounds from transformer aggregation or a weaker encoder. Why best next: Multiprofile is the largest untested structural axis; resolving whether it adds value (or not) with a clean, minimal change from config_004 will either open a promising direction for further exploitation (aggregation type, fusion) or allow us to deprioritize it and focus budget on encoder improvements or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: The strongest signal so far is the large jump from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_005: 0.650 vs config_004: 0.520, +13 pp), and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is sufficient or whether a transformer-based aggregation can further exploit the multiprofile structure. Question: config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, changing only the aggregation method. This isolates the effect of aggregation while holding the best-performing encoder and profile setting fixed. Rationale: Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because (a) it directly exploits the strongest observed direction (multiprofile + scvi), (b) it tests whether the current best can be improved along the aggregation axis, and (c) the answer determines whether all subsequent multiprofile experiments (including any multimodal ones) should use avgpool or transformer, saving future compute and guiding the search efficiently.

We now have three of four cells in a critical 2×2 factorial (encoder × profile): pca-single (0.485), scvi-single (0.520), and scvi-multiprofile (0.650–0.653). The missing cell is pca-multiprofile (config_002). This experiment directly tests whether the large multiprofile gain (~13 pts) is a general property of multi-profile aggregation or is specifically enabled by scvi_n200's learned latent representation. If pca-multiprofile also reaches ~0.65, the profile setting dominates and encoder choice becomes secondary; if it stays near ~0.50, the interaction between encoder and profile is the key driver, and future experiments should prioritize encoder selection. Resolving this interaction is the highest-information next step because it determines whether subsequent budget should be spent exploring new encoders (scgpt) in multiprofile, exploring multimodal fusion, or other directions. It also avoids changing multiple factors at once (only encoder differs from the best config_005, with aggregation held at avgpool where the transformer gain was negligible).

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile models dominate (0.59–0.65), with scvi_n200 consistently outperforming pca_n2000, and image-only models are very weak (0.21). Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has minimal impact (~0.003). Uncertainty: We have not tested scgpt, the third available RNA encoder, and it is unclear whether it can match or exceed scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting. This experiment (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, acc=0.650), isolating the encoder effect while holding profile and aggregation constant. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, it opens a new high-performing direction for subsequent multimodal experiments; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the best encoder and can redirect budget toward testing whether multimodal fusion or a stronger image encoder (ViT) adds value. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves a key untested design axis at the current performance frontier without conflating multiple changes.

Evidence: RNA-only experiments clearly establish that scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the best RNA configuration (config_006: 0.653 acc, transformer aggregation; config_005: 0.650, avgpool). The image modality is unexplored beyond a weak resnet50 baseline (config_010: 0.208 acc). The biggest remaining design uncertainty is whether adding image features via fusion can complement the strong RNA signal or will only add noise. This experiment (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests that question by pairing the best RNA setup with a stronger image encoder (ViT-L vs. the weak ResNet50) and a simple concat fusion. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it resolves the highest-impact unknown—whether multimodal fusion adds value at all—before committing further experiments to the multimodal space; (2) it uses a direct comparison to config_006 (same RNA encoder, profile, and aggregation) so the effect of adding image is isolated; (3) choosing ViT-L over ResNet50 avoids confounding a negative result with a known-weak image encoder, making the outcome more interpretable; and (4) the result will inform whether to invest remaining budget in tuning fusion strategy, image encoder, or aggregation in the multimodal setting.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI_n200, ViT_L, transformer, concat) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.721) so far, a ~7-point gain over the best RNA-only config (0.653). However, we have no evidence about whether the concat fusion is optimal or whether the two modalities have asymmetric information content that a weighted fusion could exploit. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of fusion strategy. This tells us whether the modalities contribute equally (concat sufficient) or unequally (weighted better), which is a fundamental design decision for all future multimodal experiments. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a minimal single-variable change from the current best configuration, directly comparable to config_038, and resolves an important uncertainty about how to combine modalities before investing further experiments in other design axes (aggregation, image encoder choice, or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, this clean A/B comparison maximizes information per experiment.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The multimodal configs (038/039) show a large jump from the best RNA-only result (0.653) to ~0.725, but we have only one image-only data point (ResNet50, single-profile, 0.208), which tells us almost nothing about how well the ViT-L encoder captures useful signal. We cannot yet decompose whether the multimodal gain comes from genuinely complementary image information or merely from a larger model. 2) What this tests: config_015 (image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer) isolates the image modality with the same strong encoder used in the top multimodal configs, directly measuring how much predictive signal the image carries independently. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, this single-variable test reduces the largest remaining uncertainty—whether the image branch is contributing real information or is a dead weight. If ViT-L image-only is strong (>0.5), the multimodal gain is partly additive image information and we should invest in image-side improvements; if it remains weak, the multimodal gain likely comes from cross-modal interaction, guiding us toward fusion/aggregation refinements. This knowledge is prerequisite for making informed exploitation decisions in subsequent experiments, making it more informative than marginal tweaks (e.g., concat vs weighted) that show only ~0.4% differences.
